messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I have landmark data from a population sampled in several years. For each combination of two consecutive samples, I would like to get scores for each individual along the vector joining the two samples (similar to PC scores) so that I can measure evolutionary rates along this vector in haldanes. This seems fairly simple but I couldn't find a way to do this in previous posts or the documentation for geomorph or RRPP, so apologies if this has already been asked.

thanks
Grant

messages.body_plain:
Grant,

If your PC scores are arranged as 1:n, 1:n for individual research subjects, then you can do something like this:

PC.scores <- myPCA$x
ind.vectors <- PC.scores[1:n, ] - PC.scores[((n+1):2*n), ]

If your scores are arranged as 1,1, 2, 2, …, n, n, then something like this might work:

first <- seq(1, 2*n -1, 2)
second <- seq(2, 2*n, 2)
ind.vectors <- PC.scores[first, ] - PC.scores[second, ]

Each of the rows in ind.vectors are changes in PC scores from one time to the next.  Note that I am answering your question about how to get “scores”.  I assume you know how to turn these into Haldanes.

Best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a further question regarding the bilat.symmetry
function and its output FA.component. For each individual in a dataset, one FA.component
coordinate matrix is returned. I was wondering how replicate measures of the
same individual are combined? I presume that an average shape must be found
from the replicates, but was wondering how this was achieved.

Sincerely,

Ben.

messages.body_plain:
Ben,

As stated in the help file:

“The fluctuating asymmetry component for each specimen, found as the specimen-specific side deviation adjusted for the mean directional asymmetry in the dataset.”

When there are replicates for each individual, this is based on the individual’s mean values. The last few lines of code in the function calculates these:

X.ind.side <- model.matrix(~(side:ind) + 0, data = as.data.frame(dat.shape[-1]))

    ind.mns <- coef(.lm.fit(X.ind.side, Y))

FA.component <- ind.mns[-indsq, ] - ind.mns[indsq, ]

FA.component <- simplify2array(lapply(1:n.ind, function(j) {

        t(matrix(FA.component[j, ], k, p)) + mn.shape - mn.DA

    }))

messages.body_plain:
Hello geomorph community,

I am trying to use the gm.prcomp function as described in the "Principal components analysis and visualization tools for exploring shape space", with no success.

I have a tree with 21 taxa in the newick format, I have read it with read.tree from ape. Also, I calculated my species means to run this analysis:

subset_coords_spe <- coords.subset(A = lm_data_pa$coords,
                               group = class$Species)
names(subset_coords_spe)
spmean <- lapply(subset_coords_spe, mshape)
spmean <- simplify2array(spmean, higher = TRUE)

r <- read.tree("tree.newick")
gm.prcomp(spmean, phy = r)

this is the error that I get: Error in Y[phy$tip.label, ] : índice fora de limites (index out of bounds, in english)

All the names of labels match, so I'm not sure of what might be causing this problem.

Thanks in advance,

--
Diniz Ferreira
Graduando em Ciências Biológicas
Laboratório de Evolução e Genética de Insetos (LEGIN)
DEZG - IB - Universidade Federal de Pelotas

messages.body_plain:
Faysal,

all ANOVA/regression-type tests in geomorph base their significance testing in the residual permutation procedures. They are in fact based on wrapping more general (i.e. not specific to GM coordinates) functions of the RRPP package. As such, they can be used for any kind of data for which regression-type approaches are correct, and they are bound to differ from other approaches precisely because they assess significance in a whole different way.

For more details, I suggest you read the function's help files, and Collyer, M. L. and D. C. Adams. 2018. RRPP: RRPP: An R package for fitting linear models to high‐dimensional data using residual randomization. Methods in Ecology and Evolution. 9(2): 1772-1779. https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.13029

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
Faysal,

A quick comment on the second portion of your email.

If one implements things correctly – and uses the same model choices (e.g., BM and lambda = 1 for both) - procD.pgls and ML-based PGLS via gls() should yield equivalent results.

This was demonstrated in Adams and Collyer 2018 (Evolution) for phylogenetic ANOVA. The Supplemental Information of that paper shows things empirically via simulation:  see Supp. Figs 1-2 for beta and F-values being identical, and p-values differing only due to the number of permutation iterations.  Also, Figs S4-S6 in that same SI demonstrate that the empirical F-distribution from RRPP in procD.pgls is identical to the distribution from theory.

This property also holds for phylogenetic regression.

Dean

messages.body_plain:
Hey all!

Just had a question about the use of phylo.modularity. I am trying to run it on coordinates for specimens at the family level such that each family has multiple specimens.

However, I am getting the following error:

> Art_Mod<-phylo.modularity(Art_coords_Mod,phy=U_tree_art,land.gpsA,CI=FALSE,iter=9999)
Error in phylo.modularity(Art_coords_Mod, phy = U_tree_art, land.gpsA,  :
  Tree is missing some taxa present in the data matrix

I checked the dimnames of the coordinates with the match function, but it seems like there aren't any discrepancies between them and the tip labels of the phylogeny. I checked the help file and it seems like there was only one specimen of each species analyzed, so I am wondering if phylo.modularity can't be applied to higher taxonomic levels than at the species level?

Sorry if this is a dumb question, I just can't seem to wrap my head around why it might not be working...

Kindest regards,
Austin Ashbaugh

messages.body_plain:
Austin,

Make sure you are using the match function appropriately.  The error suggests you might have all the names of tree tips in the data, but some taxa some observations in the data are not in the tree.  Here is a demo for how the match function could be misleading:

> A <- 1:6
> B <- 1:10
> match(A,B)
[1] 1 2 3 4 5 6

Everything looks fine here, but switch the two around

> match(B, A)
 [1]  1  2  3  4  5  6 NA NA NA NA

Now NAs are revealed for values in B that are not in A.  A is contained in B  but B is not contained in A.  The error suggests that the number of observations in your data exceed the taxa you have in your tree but if you did a match with tip labels preceding observation names, it would not alert you there is an issue.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi Austin,

Thanks for the clarification.  The answer to your question is simpler.

>
> Can phylo.modularity be used if there are multiple observations/specimens allocated to each tip.label?

No!

Neither phylo.modularity nor any phylogenetic comparative method can use a covariance matrix that is a species by species matrix, if the number of observations is different than the number of species.  In PCMs, the species (or other taxonomic unit) are the observations.

Mike

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] phylo.modularity at taxonomic level higher than species?
messages.body_plain:
One thing to consider, it sounds like your research question is targeting individual-level analysis but you are concerned about species differences influencing your results, as species differences would create variation among individuals (or families or whatever sub-species subject you are considering).  If that is the case, I do not think you are interested in using a PCM but should be interested in using a method that accounts for the multiple species you are using for your research.

Here is a potential solution.  Others might argue this is not appropriate and I do not feel strongly about it either, but it gets you closer to answering a specific kind of research question.

fit0 <- procD.lm(coords ~ 1, data = mydata, iter = 1, …) # estimates overall mean
fit1 <- procD.lm(coords ~ species, data = mydata, iter = 1, …) # estimates species means

sfshape <- fit0$GM$fitted + fit1$GM$residuals # overall mean plus species residuals

sfshape above is species-free shape; i.e., the effect of species has been held constant.  Perform a modularity test on this (not phylo.modularity) and variation among species will not obfuscate interpretations made at a sub-species level.

Again, this is not a PCM but if the scope of your analysis is not at the species (or other taxonomic unit) level, you should not be using a PCM.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am working with time series within two populations, and I am interested in whether the direction of shape change between sampling years changes. I know that I can measure the angles of vectors describing change across all sampling years using trajectory.analysis, but I am more interested in the angle of change between time points (i.e., does the direction of change in population A differ between time1->time2 and time2->time3?). I would also like to compare pop. A time1->time2 to pop. B time1->time2 or pop. B time2-time3, but this is less important for me than comparisons of changes between times within the same population.

I think I found a similar conversation from a while back about comparisons of vector lengths (rather than angles) between "segments" in a trajectory here <https://groups.google.com/g/geomorph-r-package/c/wbxkMp35W6o/m/7Yb47jVlAQAJ>, but I can't figure out how this would be done now that advanced.procD.lm is deprecated.

thanks
Grant

Dear community,

I would like to perform an integration.test using two 3 D data matrices of 20 and 30 landmarks respectively.

The thing is that I would like to remove the variation related to population and sex previous to analyze integration. To do so I’ve calculated the pooled-within vcv matrices using the cov.W function (Le Maitre and Mitteroecker, in press).

My question is: is there a way to perform a two.b.pls/integration.test analysis taking into account the within group variation?

Thanks in advance,

E.

messages.body_plain:
Eric,

I feel you are missing an important connection for what the pooled within-group VCV is and how it is calculated.  If one has a linear model, e.g., lm(Y ~ group), from which they obtain residuals (R), then W = crossprod(R) / df, where df is the appropriate residual degrees of freedom.  (Note: the cov.W function in the vcvComp package calculates an unweighted mean of single-group covariance matrices, irrespective of the number of observations per group, meaning small groups and large groups contribute equally to the estimate of the pooled within-group covariance matrix.  This is not consistent with the cov function in R and not something I feel is appropriate.  The two functions will produce similar covariance matrices if and only if data are balanced.  You have been warned!)

It’s the residuals that are values independent of the effect of groups, like population:sex levels.  Using such residuals in a PLS analysis should accomplish what you seek to accomplish.

If this explanation does not make sense (to anyone reading this), my first recommendation would be to become comfortable with what linear models are , what they do, and how they can be used.  Trying to understand what a residual (e.g., pooled within-group) covariance matrix is and does without understanding the linear algebra of linear models will always have limited utility.

Good luck!
Mike

Dear Geomorph Mailing List,

I am currently trying to digitize data from a number of mammalian teeth. Two of my landmarks of interest are the apices of two cusps. In most of the specimens I am digitizing, these cusps are clear, independent structures. However, there is a trend within this group for the two cusps to become increasingly connate, to the point that in some taxa the apices of the two cusps are completely indistinguishable.

I am trying to figure out a way to include these landmarks in my geometric morphometric. I had thought about simple coding the two landmarks as being the same for taxa in which the two cusps are connate, but I remember reading that this will not work for geomorph because the package cannot handle distances of zero between landmarks. Is there any way to digitize these features in a way geomorph can handle?

Sincerely,
Russell

Russell,

I’ll follow up on Antigoni’s cogent points, and focus on the last one. Landmarks are the quantitative place-holders for bits of anatomy, which minimally exhibit operational homology, but ideally evolutionary/ biological homology. From that perspective, having 2 points that are 100% coincident is illogical, as it states that this particular object has 2 identical homologous ‘bits’ of anatomy. That is rather nonsensical.

As for the analytical/computational components, these will not have a problem, with the exception of a TPS deformation grid. If you take as the reference the object with 2 coincident points, and as the target an object where these 2 points are in different locations, the TPS math will blow up. The reason is that it will literally attempt to ‘rip’ the grid apart at this point. That too states that the procedure is illogical.

I do want to make a comment too.

There are plenty of cases in development where bilaterally symmetric grow towards each other to form a single midline structure. As per Antigoni's point, you can create a paired landmark on the "fused" structure, and you can carefully jitter coordinates such that you avoid issue Dean is commenting, so that the math still works. The main problem is not so such the operational homology, but GPA being a fairly naive method of superimposition. Since it will distribute some of the variance from across other landmarks, which would undoubtedly going to be a lot more variable than those points, onto these points. In the end, you may end up in situations where these two points might be crossing over each other, which wouldn't make biological sense.

But I see that rather than being nonsensical, that a fairly big limitation of the method dealing with novelties.

Folks,

On the issue of absent or merged structures, I wish to point out that ad-hoc digitizing solutions to circumvent mathematical realities frequently do not lead to much insight. I’ll trust that by 'naive' Murat is suggesting that GPA does not weight any landmarks, a priori, as a superimposition procedure, which should not be interpreted as non-robust or flawed.  Quite simply, a garbage-in-garbage-out outcome does not mean the method is limited; it could mean it was a user error to use it in an unintended way (which I think is Murat’s point).

Absent structures in some specimens relative to others this has long been noted in both development and evolution; and is a notoriously difficult issue to deal with quantitatively. And several ad-hoc 'solutions' to this problem exist in the literature: most of which are based on double digitizing locations in some manner. But all are ad-hoc ways of circumventing the real issue, which is that the structure is either absent on some specimens, or coincident.  That is a biological problem that seeks to be addressed using some new theory, and new (and mathematically vetted) analytical procedures. Current GMM theory, and by extension GPA, is simply not equipped for such biological singularities. But this is not a GPA problem: it is a logic problem.

At present I do not have a solution to the none-into-multiple structure issue. That will require some new and creative digitizing, as well as some new analytics to accommodate such structures. But I will point out that the 'does it seem to work' criterion will not be sufficient to vett such new methods. Rather, they must adhere to strict mathematical and statistical theory; for if they provide a solution, but that solution is neither general nor robust, one is no better off than using the ocular test for comparing the two structures.

There are plenty of cases in development where bilaterally symmetric grow towards each other to form a single midline structure. As per Antigoni's point, you can create a paired landmark on the "fused" structure, and you can carefully jitter coordinates such that you avoid issue Dean is commenting, so that the math still works. The main problem is not so such the operational homology, but GPA being a fairly naive method of superimposition. Since it will distribute some of the variance from across other landmarks, which would undoubtedly going to be a lot more variable than those points, onto these points. In the end, you may end up in situations where these two points might be crossing over each other, which wouldn't make biological sense.

But I see that rather than being nonsensical, that a fairly big limitation of the method dealing with novelties.

To give some
clarification as to what is going on in my group of interest, what happens is
that ancestrally these two structures represent separate cusps on the tooth.
Throughout evolutionary history, the apices of these cusps become closer and
closer together until their tips are indistinguishable and they become one
structure. The homology between this single cusp and the two cusps of other
taxa are pretty clear if you look at the change in this feature across a
phylogeny. The distance the two cusps are apart from one another is actually a
feature of significance for me, since it seems to correlate with dietary habits
within the group (omnivores have more widely separated cusps, whereas in
carnivores the two cusps are increasingly fused).

 If it was just a few taxa that had separate cusps there wouldn't be much of a problem in just considering the landmark inapplicable, but in this case the distance between the two landmarks is actually of interest and excluding one of the two points would mean excluding a significant landmark on about 90% of the data for the sake of the remaining 10%.

Russell,

If the distance between cusps — in which a value of 0 means 0 — is important, why not measure this directly and use it as dependent variable in an analysis?  Or why not use a generalized linear model with a binomial link function to consider the probability of having one or two cusps?  It seems that your quest might be to not overlook this important attribute when describing shape differences but I think shape, number of cusps, and distance between cusps are all different attributes, and shape can only be defined for anatomical landmarks that all specimens possess.

This is not a unique problem.  In my earlier research life I used to digitize fish.  I knew that their fins were important structures for locomotion.   But to attempt to include their shape in the definition of body shape by landmarks was foolhardy, since they were flexible structures that could open or close like a fan, be easily damaged, and comprised various articulation planes.  I had to reconcile that an analysis of fin shape would have to be separate from body shape, as finding a way to fix the arbitrary positions of fin landmarks would be required.  Therefore, an analysis of body shape had to largely exclude fins, but this did not mean the evolution of fin shape was unimportant to consider.  It would just be a separate analysis

I think you have to consider not including the apex of one cusp in your definition of shape and have a separate analysis for consideration of cusp number or distance between, simply because you cannot force landmark configurations to have Cartesian coordinates for a structure that does not exist.  As a minimum, you are making an arbitrary decision that could influence your interpretations because of its effect on other landmarks, as Murat alluded.  But there is a mathematical basis for this problem that is inescapable.  If you have two landmarks in the same spot, you have 0 covariances between the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of the landmarks, which will have profound influence on the cross-products between different configurations, which means Procrustes alignment is rendered meaningless.  Murat’s suggestion to add measurement error does not completely fix this (and I don’t think he intended to imply it does), especially if the covariances created by doing this are not anatomically reasonable.  (We discussed this in our recent paper: Collyer, M. L., Davis, M. A., & Adams, D. C. 2020. Making heads or tails of combined landmark configurations in geometric morphometric data. Evolutionary Biology, 47:193-205.  It was a different purpose, regarding combining configurations, but the point is the same.  When arbitrary covariances among landmarks are introduced, one is no longer doing a “shape” analysis.)

Is one cusp moving compared to the other?  Or are they both converging toward the center?  Then digitizing the apex of one cusp, not two, will still capture the shape change of the one cusp associated with merging with another.  Rather than trying to invent landmarks for a missing structure, why not just quantify the change in shape of one structure, knowing its change in shape has something to do with the convergence of cusps?

At least doing something like that would not introduce an arbitrary mathematical nuance that GPA cannot ignore.

Mike

messages.subject: Running gpagen on a landmarking set that used coords.subset?
messages.subject_clean: Running gpagen on a landmarking set that used coords.subset?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I have a set of 2D landmarks on the dorsal cranium of individual voles from nine different populations. Since there were missing landmarks in this dataset, I used the coords.subset function to subset the whole dataset by population (so within the whole dataset, there are now nine sub-arrays). I did this since I wanted the missing landmarks to be estimated based solely on the shape of the population the individual belongs to (rather than from the shapes of individuals across all the populations combined).

To estimate the locations of these missing landmarks, I first used the fixLMmirror function from package Morpho to estimate the bilateral landmarks (since I landmarked both sides of the cranium), then used the TPS method in geomorph's estimate.missing function to fill in any remaining missing landmarks. Once completing both of those steps, I checked to make sure that no missing landmarks remained (and none were found).

Next, I needed to run a generalized Procrustes analysis before I could analyze any of the size and shape data contained in my landmarking set. But this is where I ran into a problem. When I applied the coords.subset function to my whole dataset, that converted the 3D array my dataset started as into a list of nine 3D sub-arrays (representing each population), so gpagen sent an error message telling me that "Coordinates must be a 3D array".

Is there a way to get gpagen to ignore the "list" aspect of my dataset so it can run the generalized Procrustes analysis on all the landmark coordinates within that list? Or is there a way to reconvert the list of my population arrays back into a single, ungrouped array without sacrificing the estimated landmarks I filled in? Any advice or suggestions would be greatly appreciated!!

Thanks,

Mariah

messages.subject: Phylogenetically aligned component analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues,

We wish to alert you to a new article, introducing phylogenetically aligned component analysis, currently in early release form:

Collyer, M.L. and D.C Adams. 2020 (in press). Phylogenetically aligned component analysis.  Methods in Ecology and Evolution.

If you do not have access to MEE, we have a link to the accepted article and supporting information here <https://www.researchgate.net/publication/344900621_Phylogenetically_Aligned_Component_Analysis>.  (Or paste https://www.researchgate.net/publication/344900621_Phylogenetically_Aligned_Component_Analysis in your web browser.)

Phylogenetically aligned component analysis (PACA) is an ordination method similar to principal component analysis (PCA), but aligns data to maximum phylogenetic signal rather than maximum variance.  In conjunction with PCA (or phylogenetic PCA), PACA provides a tool for visualizing phylogenetic signal in multivariate data, even if other signals (e.g., allometry, ontogenetic, ecological) might obscure phylogenetic signal in PCA.

We make PACA available to GM users in the RRPP and geomorph R packages, with RRPP::ordinate and geomorph::gm.prcomp functions.  These functions allow users to align data to either principal or phylogenetically aligned vectors, optionally transform data by phylogenetic covariances, project ancestral states and phylogenetic tree edges into a plot, and evaluate the amount of covariance between data and phylogeny, by vector.  Additionally, the physignal function in geomorph provides $PACA output, along with the amount of cumulative phylogenetic signal, by vector, which can inform if phylogenetic signal is especially strong in certain data dimensions.

We recommend installing the latest versions of RRPP and geomorph via Github; i.e.,

devtools::install_github(“mlcollyer/RRPP”, build_vignettes = TRUE)
devtools::install_github(“geomorphR/geomorph”, ref = “Stable”, build_vignettes = TRUE)

Happy computing!

Mike Collyer and Dean Adams

> One thing to consider, it sounds like your research question is targeting individual-level analysis but you are concerned about species differences influencing your results, as species differences would create variation among individuals (or families or whatever sub-species subject you are considering).  If that is the case, I do not think you are interested in using a PCM but should be interested in using a method that accounts for the multiple species you are using for your research.
>
> Here is a potential solution.  Others might argue this is not appropriate and I do not feel strongly about it either, but it gets you closer to answering a specific kind of research question.
>
> fit0 <- procD.lm(coords ~ 1, data = mydata, iter = 1, …) # estimates overall mean
> fit1 <- procD.lm(coords ~ species, data = mydata, iter = 1, …) # estimates species means
>
> sfshape <- fit0$GM$fitted + fit1$GM$residuals # overall mean plus species residuals
>
> sfshape above is species-free shape; i.e., the effect of species has been held constant.  Perform a modularity test on this (not phylo.modularity) and variation among species will not obfuscate interpretations made at a sub-species level.
>
> Again, this is not a PCM but if the scope of your analysis is not at the species (or other taxonomic unit) level, you should not be using a PCM.
